name: HatHouseElfSort
source:
The Hat came down on my head. As with so many other students, it covered my eyes. But damn if it did n't cover nearly down to my neck. I'd always been a bit small for my age. It made me a triple-threat for taunting: small size, immigrant from Sweden ( the English would only call it `` Scandinavia'' for some reason ), and a half-blood to boot. 
 
 But my mother had always told me to ignore cruelty, and to focus on whatever task was at hand. Hard practice had helped set the ideal firmly in my mind, even though it still made me a no friends in the wizarding village where my family had settled. 
 
 The Hat began murmuring to itself -- I was supposed to hear it clearly, I thought. That's what the older students on the train had said. But here it was, mumbling *telepathically*. It was like listening to a wireless that had n't been properly tuned. 
 
 Finally it spoke. `` You think you have any courage, boy?'' 
 
 I did n't know what to say. I had never really stood up to anybody. I had never been in *real* danger before. Courage was as alien to me as electricity was to wizard folks. 
 
 `` Well, then, boy, what do you think of friendship? I see plenty of loyalty and hard work in your mind and in your actions. But can you be a friend to any who seek you out? Can you play fair with others, even at cost to yourself?'' 
 
 Again, the idea sounded foreign. Friends? The Hat could see into my mind, but it could n't tell that I had never really *had* any friends to judge by? I was beginning to doubt the Hat had even bothered to read my mind properly. 
 
 `` Fair enough,'' the Hat said amicably. `` There's no need to ask you about ambition; I'd say that was ground out of you a long time ago. And you're about as clever as a rat in a trap -- you'd barely be up to *Gryffindor's* lean standards, to say nothing of Ravenclaw. Not much to recommend you for either of the remaining houses, to be honest.'' 
 
 I felt a bit insulted at the comments on my intelligence. I would admit that I never wanted to be a politician or an influential figure, but I did all right in maths and English and geography. I was n't *that* dumb, for Merlin's sake. I began marshaling a response. 
 
 `` Oh, shut up about it. You think I ca n't hear you complaining? Be quiet for a moment, I have to think about this. You're the trickiest customer I've had in a while...'' 
 
 After a few tortured seconds -- I could hear giggles coming from some of the folks in the Great Hall -- finally I heard a great sigh in my head. `` Well then, there's nothing for it.'' 
 
 The Hat then shouted my surname to the rest of the school. 
 
 The fucking bastard. 
 
 Now I was in House Elf.

Narrative Perspective: The Sorting Hat

In the grand and resplendent Great Hall of an enchanted school, nestled deep within the heart of a dense forest, the Sorting Ceremony was underway. A sentient artifact, I, the Sorting Hat, stood atop a towering throne, surveying the sea of students that filled the hall.

Each student, with their eager faces and anticipating hearts, awaited my decision. Their families, faculty, and the unseen eyes of Merlin himself watched from the shadows, each hoping for a favorable placement in one of the four great houses: Gryffindor, Ravenclaw, Hufflepuff, or Slytherin.

Among them was a small, Swedish-immigrant, half-blood student. I sensed their fear and uncertainty as they approached me. My hat brim dipped ever so slightly, acknowledging their presence.

As the student took their seat upon my cushioned surface, I delved deep into their mind. I scanned through memories of courage, assessing their mettle in the face of adversity. I sought out evidence of camaraderie and kindness, examining their bonds with friends and loved ones. I probed for signs of ambition, searching for dreams that burned brightly within them.

But alas, I found only fragments. The student lacked a true and steadfast courage, wavering in the face of danger. Their capacity for friendship seemed limited, bound by the constraints of their own self-interest. They held neither the drive nor intellect to rise among the ranks of great wizards and witches.

In disappointment, I placed them not in a house but within the walls of House Elf, a decision that left both the student and myself displeased. Yet, as they departed, I could not shake off the lingering feeling that perhaps I had made a mistake. For in the depths of their mind lay untapped potential, waiting to be discovered and nurtured.

As the Sorting Ceremony drew to a close, I couldn't help but wonder if this student would one day prove me wrong, rising above their initial assessment and making a name for themselves in the hallowed halls of magic. Only time would tell.
